idiom_name: KafkaJS producer.transaction() with typed transaction object
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime transaction semantics; the boundary comes from KafkaJS, where Kafka.producer({ transactionalId, idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 1 }) yields a transaction object from producer.transaction() that stages send/sendBatch and exposes sendOffsets for consume-transform-produce. Types help by making the staged object a different type from the base producer, so a send through the wrong handle is a compile error rather than a silent dual write. It covers broker operations only; database-coupled services use the outbox variant.
pitfalls: The producer options are easy to get wrong: without transactionalId the transaction object loses fencing, and without idempotent with maxInFlightRequests: 1 the exactly-once guarantees do not hold.
Type safety stops at the process boundary: an awaited database call inside the transaction body is still outside the broker transaction.
A transaction left open by an unhandled rejection blocks later sends until the broker times it out, so abort() belongs in every failure path.

variants.name: Prisma / node-postgres interactive transaction + outbox table
variants.idiom_name: prisma.$transaction(async tx => ...) or pg BEGIN..COMMIT + outbox row
variants.implementation_notes: The database-coupled realization: the business row and the outbox row are written through one interactive transaction (Prisma's $transaction callback or a pg client running BEGIN/COMMIT), and publication happens after the promise resolves, or from a relay that reads committed rows. It needs no transactional broker and keeps the database as the only hard dependency, which is the right shape when the queue offers no transactions or when business commits must not depend on broker availability.
pitfalls: Publishing inside the interactive transaction callback happens before COMMIT; the callback resolving is the commit point, so publish after it returns.
Prisma's interactive transaction has a default timeout of a few seconds and holds a connection, so a slow publish inside it turns into timeout errors under load.
A relay that deletes outbox rows before the broker acknowledges loses messages on delivery failure; delete only after the acknowledgement.
